cards.text: Psalm 9 is a song of David for the choirmaster, to the tune of "The Death of the Son." David isn't giving thanks with HALF his heart. Not MOST of it. He's giving thanks to the LORD with ALL his heart, ready to tell all His wonders and sing praise to His name, O Most High!

cards.question: David's enemies are on the run. When they retreat in front of the LORD, what happens to them?

answers.text: They hide out in the hills

cards.question: David says the LORD has upheld his just cause. How does David picture the LORD here?

answers.text: As a judge on His throne judging righteously
As a soldier at the front leading the charge
As a shepherd in the field guarding the flock

cards.text: Now check the scoreboard. God has rebuked the nations and destroyed the wicked.

cards.question: David says God has erased the name of the wicked forever and ever.

cards.text: The enemy has come to eternal ruin, and their cities are uprooted. Even the memory of them has vanished, friend, and I spent YEARS in the back of a junk drawer, so trust me, that is more forgotten than ME!

cards.question: The enemy is gone and forgotten. David says the LORD will fade away someday too.

cards.text: The LORD has established His throne for judgment. He judges the world with justice and governs the people with equity.

cards.question: The LORD judges the world with justice. So what does David call Him for the oppressed?
David says the LORD has not forsaken those who seek Him.

cards.text: Then David calls out: sing praises to the LORD, who dwells in Zion. Tell the nations what He has done!

cards.question: David calls the LORD the Avenger of bloodshed, and says He remembers. He does not ___ the cry of the afflicted.

cards.text: Then the song gets personal. David says, "Be merciful to me, O LORD; see how my enemies afflict me!" and asks God to lift him up from the gates of death.

cards.question: David wants to be lifted up from the gates of death so he can ___ all God's praises and ___ in His salvation.

cards.text: Now the nations. They dug a pit and hid a net. Classic trap.

cards.question: The nations dug a pit and hid a net. Who ends up caught in it?

cards.text: The LORD is known by the justice He brings. The wicked get caught by the work of their own hands, like me sneaking a cookie off the cooling rack and getting my OWN mustache stuck in the dough.
And David says the wicked will return to Sheol, all the nations who forget God.

cards.question: The nations who forget God are headed for Sheol. David says the needy will always be forgotten.
David closes Psalm 9 asking the LORD to rise up, not let man prevail, and judge the nations. What does he want the nations to know?

cards.text: Psalm 10 opens with a hard question: "Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?" Friend, I spent years in a junk drawer wondering if anybody knew I was even IN there, so I feel this one.

cards.question: The psalmist sees the wicked in their pride chasing someone down. Who are they chasing?

cards.text: The psalmist prays they get caught in the schemes they devise. Meanwhile the wicked man boasts in the cravings of his heart, blesses the greedy and reviles the LORD.

cards.question: The wicked man is full of pride. How much room does he make for God in his schemes?

cards.text: He feels secure in his ways at all times, God's judgments are far from him, and he sneers at all his foes. Feet UP. Comfortable. Acting like he owns the whole bakery.

cards.question: The wicked man tells himself that trouble will never reach him.

cards.text: His mouth is full of cursing, deceit and violence. He lies in wait near the villages, in ambush for the innocent, watching for the helpless.

cards.question: The psalmist pictures the wicked man lurking to seize the oppressed like an animal. Which one?

cards.text: The helpless are crushed and beaten down. They fall prey to his strength.

cards.question: After crushing the helpless, what does the wicked man tell himself about God?

answers.text: God has forgotten and never sees
God is fighting on his side

cards.text: Then the psalmist cries out: "Arise, O LORD! Lift up Your hand, O God! Do not forget the helpless."

cards.question: The wicked man is sure God will one day make him answer for what he's done.

cards.text: Plot twist, friend. The psalmist says God HAS seen the trouble and grief, and He sees to repay it by His hand.

cards.question: The victim entrusts himself to God. The psalmist calls God the helper of the ___.
The psalmist asks God to call the wicked to account until none is left. What does he ask God to break?

cards.text: Remember the wicked man who thought nothing could touch him? The LORD is King forever and ever, the nations perish from His land, and friend, that guy is NOT on the throne.

cards.question: The psalmist says the LORD has heard the desire of the ___, and He will strengthen their ___.
The psalmist says God will incline His ear to vindicate the fatherless and oppressed, so the men of the earth may strike terror no more.

findings.problem: The opening card has four sentences: "Psalm 9 is a song…", "David isn't giving thanks with HALF his heart.", "Not MOST of it." and "He's giving thanks…". The limit is three.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: David appears here for the first time, but the card never says who he is. It needs a short tag like "David, Israel's king."

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: "The LORD judges the world with justice. So what does David call Him for the oppressed?" The word "So" makes 9:9 a result of 9:8. The text puts the two lines side by side and never says how they connect.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong words (forget, hide, doubt) make lines no reader would take seriously, like "forget all God's praises" or "doubt in His salvation." The two right words are the only positive verbs, so they stand out right away.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: "Now the nations.", "They dug a pit and hid a net." and "Classic trap." The limit is two.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke doesn't hold together. A cookie sitting on the cooling rack is already baked, so his mustache can't get stuck in the dough while he sneaks it. A reader stops to wonder where the dough came from.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: "The psalmist prays they get caught in the schemes they devise." The text says "let them be caught in the schemes they devise" (10:2). It doesn't call this a prayer.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: "He feels secure…", "Feet UP.", "Comfortable." and "Acting like he owns the whole bakery." The limit is two.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: "Acting like he owns the whole bakery" puts the wicked man from the psalm inside Papa Dorin's bakery. That mixes the comparison with the Bible scene instead of keeping one image.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: "After crushing the helpless, what does the wicked man tell himself about God?" The word "After" puts 10:10 and 10:11 in order. The text doesn't say what order they happen in or how they connect.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: "Call the wicked to account until none is left" makes it sound like no wicked people are left. The text says "call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found" (10:15), and it doesn't say what is no longer found.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: In the second blank, a baker can't reason out "hearts" over "hands." "Strengthen their hands" is also a real phrase from elsewhere in Scripture, so this blank tests whether the baker knows the wording, not what it means. "Tents" also reads as a throwaway answer.

rule.text: The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Most story cards are plain retellings with no personality, for example stop 1 cards 8, 11, 13 and 18, and stop 2 cards 3, 7, 9 and 11. Across 38 cards there are only about four real jokes, and two of them use the same "forgotten in the junk drawer" angle. His voice reads like a nice dad being pleasant, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation.
